summary: Specifies operations and management requirements for MPLS and for applications of MPLS such as pseudowire voice and virtual private network services. The requirements were gathered from network operators with extensive MPLS experience. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists what operators need from tools that monitor MPLS paths and services. It describes requirements for finding failures, locating their cause, measuring service, and managing the network, but does not define the tools.

questions: why is icmp ping not enough for mpls lsp testing
subtitle: The operations and management capabilities operators require for MPLS paths and services.

tldr.problem: Operators needed common requirements for detecting, diagnosing, and measuring defects in MPLS networks and services based on MPLS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers requirements for automated path checks, failure localization, path characterization, service-level measurement, alarms, interworking, management interfaces, and per-LSP accounting.
tldr.outcome: It proposes no specific mechanism. The requirements are intended to guide management tools and the evolution of MPLS OAM functions.

facts.label: Examples of service-level measures
facts.value: Latency, packet loss, jitter, and defect-free forwarding

today: RFC 4377 is an Informational RFC published in February 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines requirements and does not specify an OAM mechanism.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC collects Operations and Management (OAM) requirements for MPLS and MPLS applications such as pseudo-wire voice and VPN services. Operators with experience deploying MPLS networks contributed the requirements.

The document does not propose mechanisms. It seeks a set of requirements applicable to common service-provider MPLS networks at the time of writing, for use in network-management tools and future protocol work.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC collects operator requirements for monitoring and managing MPLS networks. It describes what tools should support, not how to build those tools.

sections.title: Detecting, Diagnosing and Characterizing Defects
sections.content:
Detection of a broken Label Switched Path (LSP) MUST be automated and must not require manual checks of every Label Switching Router along the path. Operators need to set the detection frequency and know the detection-time bounds so automated responses fit within the applicable service-level agreement.

An ICMP ping may give false results: the packet can leave the LSP, or it may not follow the same equal-cost multi-path route as customer traffic. OAM packets MUST follow the customer data path, including relevant path permutations. A path trace should identify the routers and links used and support recursive paths and equal-cost multi-path cases. Path characterization should reveal forwarding behavior such as TTL handling and label-stack operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need automated tests that follow the same path as customer traffic. A test that takes a different path can report a fault that does not exist or miss one that does.

sections.title: Service-Level Measurements and Alarms
sections.content:
OAM mechanisms are required to measure latency, packet loss, jitter, and whether forwarding is defect-free. These measurements can use separate probes, user traffic, or a combination. The measurement method SHOULD have minimal impact on network resources.

Operators MUST be able to configure how often OAM functions run, and probe rates should be coordinated or identified to reduce inconsistent results. Network elements MUST suppress or aggregate unnecessary alarms. Mechanisms are also needed to coordinate responses when several MPLS applications are affected by one defect.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need measurements of delay, loss, and variation, with probes that do not consume too many resources. When one defect affects many services, alarms and recovery actions need coordination.

sections.title: Interworking, Management and Accounting
sections.content:
An LSR that carries another network technology over MPLS MUST translate an MPLS defect into the native technology's error condition. Fault recovery SHOULD be automatic, and operators SHOULD detect and possibly correct faults before customers do. Common management interfaces are needed, including MIB modules for new OAM functions or tools.

The RFC calls for detecting denial-of-service attacks against the data and control planes as part of security management. It also requires accounting per LSP for network design, service-level verification, and inter-AS services. LSPs need a common identifier that is unique to each LSP; merged LSPs require a way to distinguish flow sources.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS should report failures in the form expected by a service carried over it. Operators also need common management interfaces and traffic measurements associated with individual paths.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Mechanisms that meet these OAM requirements must prevent unauthorized use and provide a way for operators to prevent denial-of-service attacks that use the mechanisms themselves. LSP mis-merging can have security consequences in addition to being a network defect.

Diagnostic and path-characterization tools reveal details about network construction. The RFC notes that operators MAY consider this information private.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM tools must be protected against unauthorized use and abuse. Their diagnostic results can reveal network details that operators may want to keep private.
